Solution 2 has the correct answer, $k = 10^{225}-1$.

- **Solutions 1 and 3 are wrong.** Any $10^{225}$ consecutive integers contain a good number. For $q\cdot 10^{225}+r$ with $0 \le r < 10^{225}$, the digit sum is $s(q)+s(r)$, and $s(r)$ takes every value in $\{0,\dots,2025\}$, so it covers all residues mod 2025. The set of good numbers is therefore syndetic, and no arbitrarily long bad blocks exist.
- **Lower bound:** $\{1,\dots,10^{225}-2\}$ has digit sums at most $2024$, so none is good. Hence $k \ge 10^{225}-1$.
- **Upper bound:** A bad run of length $10^{225}-1$ would require two consecutive good numbers exactly $10^{225}$ apart. That would force the extreme values in neighbouring blocks to coincide, which fails because each residue class contains more than one element of $[0,10^{225})$. So the largest bad run has length $10^{225}-2$, and $k = 10^{225}-1$ works.

I did not verify the digit count of the long 9-string in Solution 2's boxed answer; I am taking it to be $10^{225}-1$ as the proof states.

CHOICE: 2
